title: Quoting Nilay Patel
content:
The products aren't good enough to sell people on the costs.

You cannot tell people that you have to listen to the whine of a data center in their backyard for AI overviews and some of the most hilarious deep fake slop in history.

It's not worth it. It just isn't worth it to anyone. And agents aren't real and they might not be being used the way that anyone wants them to yet. All these companies are spending more than they're making on these products. Refrigerators holding blood storage in Europe are being hacked.

The costs are too high. The benefits are not real. And if you connect that to corruption, you're like, in order to impose these costs on me, these CEOs are in the White House shaking Trump's hand, renaming it to the Gulf of America, paying for this ballroom that we don't want. It's obvious crypto-corruption, and it's still slop.

The AI industry will not get out of it until they make better products. Until everyone can see without needing to be convinced, without needing an ad campaign, without any of this stuff that just using these products makes your life better.

— Nilay Patel, The Vergecast: Big Tech lost big in the 2026 election

title: Apple Support: ‘About the Illuminated Apple Logo on MacBook Pro With PROLED XDR Display’
content:
Apple Support:

To make the Apple logo dark in all lighting conditions, you can turn off its illumination using Terminal, which is in the Utilities folder of your Applications folder. You can also use Spotlight to find and open it.

Type or paste this command in Terminal, then press Return:

sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0

[...]

To turn logo illumination on again, enter this command in Terminal:

sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode

Apple might make this a GUI setting, but if I were them, I’d keep it this way. Make the people without fun in their souls use the Terminal command.

(Keeping it as a defaults setting also helps emphasize that you save no meaningful battery life by turning it off. If this gets exposed as a GUI preference, I could see it spreading as a dumb-ass “pro tip” to turn it off to save battery life, like the unshakeable utterly wrongheaded belief millions hold that they should religiously force-quit apps on iOS, when in fact doing so chews up more energy when the apps get relaunched from a cold start.)

title: Writing English is Solved
content:
Maybe you still struggle to write in Pulaar, or in your rinky-dink language. But here in the AI-connected, English-speaking world, we don't need to write anymore. In fact, I don't remember the last time I wrote English. I have one master agent that I talk to and tell what I need to get done. It breaks down the tasks and serves them to spawned agents that get the work done.

I spend $3,000 a month on tokens. I use them mostly for:

  • Research and search
  • Summarization and transcription
  • Writing (the big one)
  • Art and music

My great transition this year, as a programmer, was that once I accepted that AI can merge code without needing my review, I could let go. What this meant was that when AI writes English for me, I no longer need to review it before publishing. It can write English, and it writes it well.

Okay, let me add this here before I go too far: /s.

I read this blog post yesterday, and I'm always baffled to hear technical people write these words:

Writing code is solved.

As a software engineer who uses AI, I feel like I must be holding it wrong. I've found a correlation between the number of lines of code written and the number of bugs found. Whether a person or a model generates the code, the longer the PR, the higher the odds of finding an issue. So when someone says coding is solved, I automatically assume they were mediocre at best before using these tools.

If we look at it technically, we could say, in the same vein, that writing English is solved. The AI can write correct sentences, write paragraphs, or publish an entire document. If you have doubts about the content, you can have a second AI verify it and fix potential hallucinations. But of course, that's not how it works in the real world. The moment people detect AI-generated text, even if it is after reading the whole text, they reject it.

It feels empty, deceitful. What is an anecdote from an LLM to convey, when the experience never actually happened? Yes, code is not to be consumed like English. It is for the machine. But it is subjective in its purpose because we humans have to read it eventually.

Writing code is not solved, just as writing English cannot be solved. Writing is subjective and has no solution because it isn't a problem. If anything, AI for writing is a testament to this saying:

"Je n'ai fait celle-ci plus longue que parce que je n'ai pas eu le loisir de la faire plus courte." — Blaise Pascal

title: A video game which caused real world violence
content:
There has been a dramatic fall in the amount of interpersonal violence in most countries.

I don't want to go too Freakanomics and, obviously, correlation is not causation but perhaps video games have a role to play in this? A teenager being cooped up in their room means less exposure to situations where hormonal impertinence is likely to cause a violent reaction. Shouting and screaming at people via a headset rarely leads to real-life consequences. Beating up street-fighters is less risky than being in a street fight yourself.

But there are times when games do cause problems away from the screen. Players of Pokémon Go ramble about outside trying to collect digital pets - this also causes them to trespass into military bases.

I was recently reminded of one of the first Augmented Reality Games - Mozzies. Back in 2004 having a phone with a camera was almost unheard of. The Mozzies game let you see virtual mosquitoes overlayed on the real world - and then shoot them.

Waving your cameraphone around while playing caused at least one case of physical violence.

Here's a report from Singapore's The New Paper on 6 October 2004.

I'm grateful to Esme Potatoes for helping me find a transcript.

Playing game or snapping girl? Then… SMASH!

The incident happened while he and his friends were at Orchard Cineleisure for a movie recently.

Before the movie started at 7pm, his friends went to E-Zone, an arcade in the same building. The Indonesian student, who has lived in Singapore for more than 10 years, preferred to wait outside and play his favourite game, Mozzies, on his Siemens phone.

The game, which involves killing mosquitoes that appear on screen, requires the use of the phone's camera.

The camera captures a live video image as the game's playing background, with the mosquitoes appearing in the foreground.

The player has to move the phone around to target the mosquitoes.

Heriyono said: "I was so engrossed with the mosquitoes, I became oblivious to my surroundings."

"Then, I saw through the phone, a figure behind the swarm of mosquitoes heading in my direction but I thought he was just passing by."

Heriyono claims the man then shouted: “Trying to take a photo of my girlfriend, is it?”

And he smashed the phone on the floor.

Heriyono said he told the man, whom he estimates to be in his mid- or late 20s, that it was a misunderstanding and that he could check the phone for himself to see if he had indeed taken pictures of the man’s girlfriend.

But the phone was so badly damaged it could not be turned on.

“I was really shocked. He was behaving very aggressively, I thought he was going to hit me,” Heriyono said.

MAN WALKED OFF

But the man then walked off with his girlfriend, he said.

Heriyono and his friends decided not to chase after the man because he was older and they were worried he could get violent.

Heriyono did not make a police report either.

He was worried the man may get to him again, and refused to be photographed for this report.

When contacted, Siemens Mobile said it has never received any complaints about the games on its handphones. (See other report.)

The Mozzies game is available only on the Siemens SX1 model.

Heriyono had bought the handphone about four months earlier for over $700, after convincing his parents that it would be worth it because he uses all its functions, including the radio and MP3 player.

And he particularly liked the Mozzies game.

“In the end, the game caused me so much trouble,” he said with a sigh.

He sent the phone to the Siemens service centre but was told it was beyond repair.

His friends told him later that his actions could have looked suspicious.

“I realised that I could have looked like a pervert if seen by a passer-by,” he admitted.

“The thrill took over basic common sense and I began pointing my camera around.”

The girl was playing “air hockey” with her boyfriend at the time.

Miss Nalia Suli, 18, the receptionist at E-Zone, said she saw the commotion.

She said: “The girl was dressed very sexily. Her skirt was very short and when she bent down to pick up the ball, you could see her underwear.”

She, too, thought Heriyono was taking pictures of the girl.

“If he wasn’t taking pictures, why was the camera facing up?”

But Heriyono said: “Yes I could have pointed to the floor. But the mosquitoes are everywhere on the screen, you have to move around to kill them.”

He is now using a handphone he has borrowed from a friend, until he saves up enough to buy another. “I think after this incident, I will buy a much cheaper phone,” he said.

Perhaps staying inside to play games is safer all round!

title: Static site generators are weird
content:
I love static sites. Pre-rendered files are usually faster, lower maintenance, easier to secure, and more. Static site generators let you create these sites much more easily, which is fabulous.

But I believe most static site generators are weird.

SSGs like Jekyll, Gatsby, and Hugo require you to learn their special way of doing things. You have to answer questions like:

  • How do you write HTML templates?
  • How do you manage CSS and JavaScript?
  • How do you deal with images and videos?
  • How do you manage routing?
  • How do you generate RSS feeds?
  • How do you do unusual things, like one-off pages or redirects?

You have to understand many of these in order to build a production-ready site, and every SSG is a different world.

For example, my blog (which you’re reading right now!) has used Jekyll, Gatsby, and Hugo. For each one, I’ve had to learn its templating system, its asset system, its RSS feed system, and much more. Each project is thoughtfully designed, but totally its own thing.

That’s not to mention the majority of SSGs, which are custom-made for one website. These projects tend to overflow with personality—rare programming languages, jagged feature sets, and flowery READMEs are on fine display here—and are often prime examples of the atypical. Weirdness at its best.

This is not a critique of any particular project or of SSGs in general. I think this a lot of this weirdness is essential complexity, which I think most SSG developers would tell you. But I still think they’re weird!

I expect to receive some feedback on this post like, “Static site generator X isn’t weird! Everything it does is normal!” I haven’t had that experience, and I envy you.

Static site generators are great. And being weird is good! And I think static site generators are weird.

title: Weekend at Bernie’s II
content:
Six months after Weekend at Bernie’s, 421 of the critical repos that were dead, dormant or unknown in May are active again. In the 1993 sequel, Bernie is brought back by a voodoo ceremony that goes slightly wrong, and the result is a corpse that moves whenever it hears music. In nearly a quarter of the revived repos the music shows up in the commit history as a coding agent, with most of those commits made by the repo’s own top committer.

In the previous post I sorted the repos behind the ecosyste.ms critical packages into four buckets, and a follow-up went through the ways a project ends up dead:

  • Active: regular non-bot commits to the default branch, or a release, in the past year.
  • Dormant: little or no development, but someone with write access has closed an issue, merged a PR or pushed a commit in the past year.
  • Dead: archived, or with issues and PRs filed in the past year and no response from anyone with write access.
  • Unknown: no issues, PRs or activity in the past year, so responsiveness hasn’t been tested.

In the previous post I predicted that AI-assisted vulnerability discovery was about to test the quiet ones: “The first security report against any of them will be that test.” I re-ran the same pipeline with the same classifier at the start of November, and the headline split is within two points of May’s:

  May November change
critical repos 5,874 6,106 +232
active 48.8% 49.9% +1.1
dormant 20.2% 18.7% -1.5
dead 12.1% 11.8% -0.3
unknown 18.9% 19.5% +0.6
dead and archived 322 361 +39
dead and not archived 😎 391 361 -30
advisories with no patched version 110 133 +23

Running May’s classifier over November’s data changes only 23 buckets, so the changes come from activity in the repos, plus older issues and releases dropping out of the one-year window. 421 repos went from dormant, dead or unknown to active, and 295 that were active, dormant or unknown in May are now dead.

Who came back

Registry maintainer lists changed on the packages of only 16 of the 421 revived repos. Checked against the commit history, one of those is a renamed account, seven are staff rotating inside organisations like Docker and Google, and two added an account with no commits since, which leaves six where a new person took on the work. The registry maintainer lists were unchanged on the other 405. Abandoned-package policies at most registries are built around transferring a dead package to a new owner, one of the few ways projects change hands, and ownership changes were rare among these revivals.

To see what those returning maintainers were working with, I ran CHAOSS’s disclosure tool over every commit in the 416 revived repos hosted on GitHub, covering the year since last November, which is the same measurement I ran across the whole critical set in August. It matches co-author trailers, agent bot emails, agent branch names and similar signals, so the numbers are a lower bound.

In the six months before May, 3.3% of human-authored commits in those repos carried an AI disclosure, spread over 22 repos. In the six months since, it was 7.9% over 95 repos, 778 commits in all, and 566 of them came from each repo’s own top committer, usually with a Claude Code trailer. Every disclosed AI commit in the dead and unknown revivals dates from after May, and 10 of the 47 dead ones and 8 of the 64 unknown ones have them.

The heaviest agent users among the revivals include:

  • python-json-patch and lz4 were both dormant in May, and have 123 and 75 agent-assisted commits.
  • rack-proxy was dead. Jacek Becela, who wrote it, has made 39 agent-assisted commits since, the repo now has a CLAUDE.md and an AGENTS.md, and it shipped 1.0.0 in July as “the modernization + security-hardening release”, 2.0.0 in September with HTTP framing hardening, and 1.0.3 as a security patch for the 1.x line.
  • net-sftp was dead and has 29 agent-assisted commits, a mix of Codex and Claude Code.
  • CEnum.jl, a Julia package that was dead in May, has 27.
  • zip-archive, a Haskell package that was unknown in May, now has 16.

My read of these commit logs is that the agents made the backlog on a finished-but-neglected library small enough to clear, and the maintainers who already knew the code were the ones best placed to check what the agent produced. Running the scan also turned up two gaps in the tool’s detection, and I’ve sent fixes for both.

Fixes and advisories

Maintainers released fixes for vulnerabilities in their own code in 43 of the revived repos since May. Where the maintainer also published a repository advisory, 19 of 20 went up within a day of the fixed release, and the wait came afterwards, while the advisory was in GitHub’s queue for review into the global Advisory Database:

  • crass, a Ruby CSS parser, had its last issue, PR or commit more than a year before May. Ryan Grove released 1.0.7 on 25 June with fixes for four denial-of-service bugs and published the four repository advisories the same day. They reached the reviewed database 116 to 125 days later, including GHSA-6wmf-3r64-vcwv on 20 October.
  • decode-uri-component had been dead since 2022. Sam Verschueren rewrote the decoder and published GHSA-vcc3-ghjq-m6fr on 29 June, and it was reviewed 63 days later. A second fix and advisory on 23 October, GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f, were reviewed within a week.
  • moment shipped 2.31.0 on 15 September with a fix for a path traversal through crafted locale names, and published GHSA-4p3w-j4w9-5jqw the same day, which was reviewed two weeks later. Matt Johnson-Pint wrote 41 of the 68 commits since July.
  • rubyntlm, dead in May, released 0.6.6 on 9 September to fix an authentication bypass where NTLMv2 responses were being verified against an empty password. Its repository advisory went up the same day, and two months later it is still missing from the reviewed database.

GitHub wrote about the backlog in June. Private vulnerability reports went from about 550 a week in January to more than 3,000 a week for most of May, and “since mid-April, due to this surge, we have not consistently met our internal goals for publication.”

Across the 1,011 advisories since May that have both a repository advisory and a dated fix, the median gap between the fixed release and the maintainer’s advisory is zero days in every bucket. The median wait from there to the reviewed database was 11 days for repos that were active in May and 38 days for repos that were dormant, dead or unknown. Dependabot and npm audit read the reviewed database, so during that wait the users of a revived package get no alert, even though the fixed version and the maintainer’s advisory are both public.

GitHub says it prioritises review by “project impact and severity”. The previously inactive repos waited longer in every severity band, and the ten of their advisories published in June waited 81 days on average, against 17 for advisories from active repos published the same month. That’s 20 advisories in all, five of them from crass, so it’s a pattern and not proof, and my guess is that a package with years of silence in its repo scores low on project impact.

Six of the 43 fixes have an AI tool visible in a release note, branch name or commit:

  • fribidi, dormant in May, lists “Security and robustness fixes found by an automated scan (Anthropic’s OSS Scanner)” in its 1.0.18 release, including an out-of-bounds write.
  • The maintainers of Spock and ruby-domain_name merged codex/ branches.
  • openid_connect has a Copilot Autofix commit, and ssl_verify_fun and iqlusioninc/crates have Claude-authored ones.

Unanswered reports

Of the 1,086 repos that were unknown in May, 189 got an outside issue or PR since then, which is the test the previous post described. In 94 of them a maintainer closed or merged something, and 17 more had maintainer commits while the outside item went unanswered. The other 78 had no maintainer activity and moved to the dead bucket. Of the 1,171 repos that were dormant in May, which I flagged in the previous post as the bigger worry, 107 are now dead and 310 are active, about three revivals for every new death.

1,345 advisories were published against packages in the set between May and November, and 8.5% of the repos that were active in May got at least one, against about 1% of dormant and dead repos and 0.3% of unknown ones. Those rates count reports that became public, and a public advisory needs someone to receive the private report, write the fix and publish the advisory alongside the release. A private report sent to an unattended repo reaches an advisory database only if the reporter publishes it themselves, so the low rate on dead repos is a poor measure of how many reports they received.

In July a security engineer at Datadog opened an issue on gojsonschema, a Go library with about 30,000 dependent repos, saying they’d found what they believed were vulnerabilities and asking the maintainers to turn on GitHub’s private vulnerability reporting or share a contact address, and it has had zero comments since. Other reporters filed publicly instead: one now-dead repo has two open issues titled “[security disclosure]”, another has two titled “Security Advisory”, and all four are unanswered. Finding someone to send a report to is one of the steps I built Scrutineer to handle, because AI scanners have made finding the bugs the easy part.

The repos that were active, dormant or unknown in May and are now dead without being archived have 250 open pull requests from outside contributors, all opened in the same six months. I scanned the 103 I could reach on the formerly unknown repos, and 24 disclose AI use, in a trailer, a branch name, or a line like “Drafted with OpenAI Codex.” at the bottom of the description. Those 103 PRs are open against 59 repos, and the latest release on each of them predates May.

Between the end of August and the start of September, Oskar Eichler sent pull requests, most of them from codex/ branches, to at least 14 Ruby and JavaScript repos in the set: small fixes and hardening changes, some with a severity like [MEDIUM] in the title. The maintainers of net-sftp, which was dead in May, merged 15 of them, and the maintainers of net-scp merged 10. The ones on repos that are dead now have had no maintainer reply since they were opened.

On faye’s websocket-extensions-ruby, James Coglan replied within a day asking what bug the changes fixed, and said the project doesn’t accept code authored by LLMs or agents without meaningful human input. Eichler closed all seven PRs there himself, saying he couldn’t honestly provide that context. As with the AI scanner findings against curl I wrote about in May, the project had a stated policy to point to.

Releases

Of the 3,198 packages in the set that were dormant, dead or unknown in May, 348 have had a new version published since and 2,850 have not. Counted by repo, maintainers published a release for 322 of the 421 revived repos, and on the other 99 the commits and merged PRs since May are unreleased. Until those releases ship, the patching and forking workarounds are the remaining option, and each downstream user has to apply them separately.

In the previous post I counted 110 advisories with no patched version, and the same measure gives 133 now. Two more are on packages whose metadata has no repository URL, which makes 135, and most of them come from how advisories are keyed: an advisory counts as unpatched per package name, so when maintainers rename a project or adopt a new major version path, every advisory on the old name counts as unpatched even when the advisory lists the fix under the new one.

  • 61 have a fix recorded in the advisory itself under a different package: phpoffice/phpexcel alone has 19 that were fixed in PhpSpreadsheet, netty 3 has 9 fixed in netty 4’s modules, and github.com/docker/docker has 4 fixed in github.com/moby/moby/v2.
  • 17 are against end-of-life lines whose advisories omit the successor, like log4j 1.x and jackson-mapper-asl.
  • 15 describe behaviour that’s by design or documented, and 9 are misattributed or about code removed years ago.
  • 4 were rejected or disputed by NVD, and 4 are versions that were published with malware in them.

25 advisories have no fix in any version, and 20 of those are on active repos. Debian marks 57 of the 135 as resolved in its own packages, and language registries, which work like Debian unstable, have no equivalent downstream packager.

Archived and deleted

44 repos in the set were archived since May, which closes the project on the record instead of leaving the issue tracker open. webpack archived six of its loaders and plugins, including css-loader and copy-webpack-plugin, several with a final commit pointing users at the equivalent now built into webpack. jsdom marked cssstyle and js-symbol-tree as unmaintained, and rust-lang archived lazy-static with a deprecation notice and cfg-if alongside it. Those ten packages have about 16 million dependent repos between them.

Fourteen repos behind critical packages have been deleted, and seven of them belonged to substack, whose GitHub account is also gone: wordwrap, text-table, commondir, archy, semver-compare and two more. Those packages still install from npm, where six of the seven list a single maintainer, nopersonsmodules, and that npm account is the only remaining place to send a report or ask for a release. The classifier reads issue data from the repo, so all fourteen are classified as unknown regardless of how many reports they receive.

See you in another six months. Until then, be suspicious of any dependency wearing sunglasses indoors.

title: How Do Building Codes Affect the Price of Housing?
content:
A great deal of effort has gone into understanding the regulatory burden on housing construction, and the extent to which it contributes to high housing prices. Much of this work is, in one form or another, about understanding how regulations restrict the supply of new housing. Harvard’s Ed Glaeser, for instance, one of the most prominent urban economists working today, has studied extensively the degree to which land-use and other regulations drive up housing prices. Likewise, the widespread YIMBY movement is largely focused on changing land-use rules to make housing abundant and affordable.

But land-use restrictions aren’t the only vehicle by which regulation can make housing more expensive; regulation can also affect housing costs by driving up the costs of producing it. While there are a variety of regulations that could potentially do this, the biggest regulatory driver of housing costs is almost certainly building codes. Virtually every jurisdiction in the US has some sort of exhaustive list of requirements that any building erected must meet. Given that construction costs make up the largest fraction of the costs of building new housing in the US, it’s useful to understand the extent to which these costs are affected by building codes.

How building codes work

I’ve previously written about how building codes work in the US, so I’ll just give a brief overview here. At a high level, most building code adoption is handled at the state level, though there are various exceptions. Some sub-state jurisdictions like cities or counties will adopt stricter rules on top of the state’s minimum requirements, or occasionally adopt their own code entirely. Beyond that, it can be a jumble. Some states have no statewide building code for certain building types, and leave it up to local jurisdictions. Manufactured homes are governed by a federal building code. And so on.

On the whole, jurisdictions don’t typically author their own code from scratch; instead, most will start with a model code produced by some private organization. Almost every state in the US, for instance, has adopted some flavor of the International Building Code (IBC), authored by the International Code Council (ICC), whose codes, despite the name, are used almost solely in the US.

Building codes will specify various requirements that a building must meet, often in exhaustive detail. Which sorts of materials you’re allowed to use for which sorts of buildings. The minimum size and dimensions of various rooms. How you must protect a building from fire. How much and what sorts of insulation you need. The list goes on, and on, and on.

Code-authoring organizations typically update these codes on a regular cycle: the International Building Code, for instance, is updated every three years. Jurisdictions will in turn update the version of the code they’re using every so often, though generally less frequently than the model code updates. Georgia, for instance, updates most of its codes every six years.

For housing, the two most important building codes are probably the International Residential Code (IRC), a model code for one- and two-family homes, and the International Building Code, a model code that covers the construction of larger buildings. Virtually every jurisdiction in the US has adopted some version of these two codes. Other important codes are the Uniform Mechanical Code and Uniform Plumbing Code, from the International Association of Plumbing and Mechanical Officials; the International Energy Conservation Code (IECC); and the National Electrical Code, from the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA).

Before we look at the costs of various code requirements, it’s important to keep in mind the proper counterfactual. The absence of a building code almost certainly wouldn’t mean “you’re allowed to build whatever you want with no restrictions.” Instead, the absence of regulation would mean a lot of de facto regulation in the form of things like insurance or mortgage lender requirements. These sorts of requirements already exist today, in the form of things like Factory Mutual insurance standards and the UK’s Professional Consultant’s Certificate, and would become more and more binding the less restrictive regulations were. Similarly, the legal responsibilities of professions like engineers and architects would also likely require buildings to meet various minimum standards in the absence of other regulations.

The cost effects of building codes

Most studies of building code cost effects look at costs relative to some baseline, typically an earlier version of the code. The most frequent and thorough (though probably somewhat biased) examinations of the cost of code requirements I’m aware of are done by the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), a homebuilder trade association that puts an enormous amount of effort into keeping the cost of building new homes as low as possible.1 Whenever a new version of the International Residential Code is released, the NAHB will issue a report that examines every code change and its likely effect on the cost of building a house. Because different provisions will affect houses in different regions differently — a changed requirement for how much snow a roof must support likely won’t affect a house built in Florida — these reports will look at the effects on several reference houses, each one the same size but built in a different area of the country. The NAHB has been issuing these reports since 2009, so they give us a good look at the last 20 years of code changes for single-family home construction.

The chart below shows an example of some of these analyses for the 2015 IRC. Some of the changes add cost: a requirement for bigger footings in certain cases and a requirement for different sorts of duct seams both added an estimated few hundred dollars to the cost of construction. Other changes reduced cost: the removal of the requirement for pipe insulation on certain pipes reduced construction cost by a few hundred dollars. So the 2015 IRC might actually raise or lower your construction costs compared to the 2012 IRC, depending on the sort of house you are building.

The chart below shows the high and low estimates for each climate zone for each version of the IRC analyzed. You can see that there’s a lot of variation, depending on the year and the area the house is built in, and even within a single area there could be a lot of variation between the high and the low estimates. In the most recent version of the IRC, the changes collectively actually reduced construction costs across the board, due to adjustments like reducing the required thickness for vapor barriers (material put in walls, floors, and the like to prevent moisture from seeping into the building).

(It’s worth noting that the 2009 IRC cost estimates include the fire sprinkler requirements that, in practice, have not been widely adopted by jurisdictions thanks to lobbying by the NAHB.)

If you take the average cost increase for the high and low estimates across the different climate areas and adjust each year for inflation, you find that, since 2006, changes to the IRC have added about $40,000 to the price of a new home. Since, per the Census Bureau, the average construction cost of a home the size of a reference home in 2024 was about $440,000, this means that, according to the NAHB, stricter code requirements have driven up home construction costs by about 0.5% per year.

Another analysis of the collective cost of code changes, but for the International Building Code, was done by Michael Eriksen, Deniz Besiktepe, and Claudio Martani in a paper published earlier this year. This paper looks at the cost effects on three-story apartment buildings of each of the 140 revisions made to the International Building Code from 2012 through 2021. In total, 16 provisions were found to raise the costs of three-story apartment buildings, out of 36 total cost-increasing provisions: the other 104 provisions were determined to be cost neutral. The authors found that the cumulative code changes raised costs by 9.9%, or about 0.8% per year.

In both the NAHB analyses and the Eriksen et al. paper, the largest cost increases come from a relatively small number of provisions. Eriksen et al. found that of the roughly $400,000 worth of cost increases between 2012 and 2021, $180,000 came from a single change: a requirement, added to the 2018 IBC, to monitor the project for fire during nonworking hours while it’s under construction. Likewise, of the 89 IRC changes that were found to be cost-increasing by the NAHB between 2009 and 2024, almost 60% of the total cost increase came from just 10 provisions.

In addition to these analyses, the NAHB also does periodic surveys of homebuilders on their perceptions of the cost of various regulations. Included in these surveys is a question asking respondents to estimate the cost of the last 10 years of building code changes, the results of which are shown below. According to these surveys, building code changes are increasing costs by around 1% per year on average, though with significant variation from developer to developer. It’s worth noting that because these are based on perceptions rather than any sort of detailed analysis, the potential for bias in these estimates is strong.

These analyses look at collective code changes, but there have also been several analyses that look at the costs of individual changes to the building code. Probably the most common change analyzed is the cost of adding fire sprinklers to homes or apartments. A 2005 National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) study estimated that fire sprinklers would add anywhere from $635 to over $2,000 to the costs of building a home, depending on the type of sprinkler system and the type of home it was installed in. The NFPA similarly looked at the costs of fire sprinklers in single-family homes in studies in 2008 and 2013. Unlike the NIST study, which was based on cost projections, the NFPA studies looked at the costs actually incurred for homes around the country that were built with fire sprinklers. The NFPA studies found an even wider variation, with additional costs ranging from less than $2,000 to more than $20,000 in 2013. Interestingly, the NFPA found that costs were substantially lower in communities with statewide sprinkler requirements compared to states where they weren’t required at the state level, suggesting that state-level requirements can drive down costs, possibly via increasing installer experience or some sort of scale effect.

One drawback with these examinations is that they’re all only looking at one side of the ledger: the costs of code requirements. But a code requirement should, ideally, have benefits as well: the costs of fire sprinklers should be somewhat offset by the benefits of reduced fire damage and fewer injuries or deaths. Even an expensive code provision might be worth it if its benefits are much higher, and a provision with a modest cost increase might nevertheless be unjustifiable if it doesn’t bring commensurate benefits.

The benefits of code requirements are also important to note because they often go unaccounted for in analyses of construction costs or construction productivity, even ones that try to adjust for changes in quality. The Census Bureau’s constant-quality price index, which tracks the cost of building single-family homes, adjusts for things like number of bedrooms and bathrooms, exterior wall material, and heating system, but not for any code-required safety changes. By contrast, the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ price index for new vehicles does take into account these sorts of legally mandated safety changes. If benefits are generally substantially higher than code costs but going unmeasured, this could partly explain construction’s stagnant productivity growth.

There have been a few cost-benefit analyses of various building code provisions. NIST followed up its 2005 study of sprinkler costs with a 2007 cost-benefit analysis of home fire sprinklers, finding benefit-cost ratios ranging from 2.4 to 6, with most of the benefits coming from averted fire deaths.

Similarly, a great deal of attention has been paid to the code requirement that multistory apartment buildings have two stairways with a corridor connecting them for egress purposes, and opposition to this provision is largely based on the fact that it adds significant cost but little in the way of benefits. A 2025 study by the Center for Building in North America notes that the second stair can add 6–13% to the cost of a building (due to the additional floor area required), while adding little to nothing in the way of improved safety. The Center for Building in North America has also put out a report on the high costs of building elevators, noting that among the cost drivers is that elevators must be large enough to fit a full-sized stretcher, though the safety benefit of this requirement is questionable.

A 2020 FEMA report performed a cost-benefit analysis of the National Flood Insurance Program requirements, which require houses in flood zones to be built some minimum elevation above the expected flood level to reduce flood damage. It found that benefits often exceeded costs, though it depended on the discount rate and the type of foundation being constructed.

And a 2019 report from the National Institute of Building Sciences looked at the benefit-cost ratios of ICC code requirements for flood, wind, and earthquake resistance and found ratios of 6 to nearly 12 compared to 1990s baselines.

There have also been several examinations of the costs of changes made to the IECC, a code that most US states have adopted and that mandates various energy-saving features like levels of insulation and degree of air sealing. The Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) has done several analyses of the costs and benefits of different iterations of this code. It found benefit-cost ratios ranging from just under 2 to over 10, depending on the year and the assumptions used for things like the discount rate.

The NAHB has also done its own analysis of the costs and benefits of the 2021 IECC, finding (unsurprisingly) a benefit-cost ratio of less than 1. The difference mostly comes from the NAHB’s higher estimates of up-front construction costs than PNNL’s. Another study of the 2021 IECC, done by a consultant for the Institute for Market Transformation, found results somewhat similar to PNNL’s.

Conclusion

While the costs of building code requirements haven’t been as thoroughly studied as other effects of housing regulation, there have been enough analyses to draw some tentative conclusions. Most studies find that modern building code changes add costs at a rate of about 0.5% to 1% per year, though with significant variation depending on the code version. Costs seem to be concentrated in a relatively small number of provisions.

However, many of these analyses only look at the costs of code changes, without considering the benefits. Likewise, many productivity analyses also fail to consider building code-induced quality increases when estimating construction output, and so may systematically underestimate productivity gains. Some code provisions, such as the requirement that multistory apartment buildings have two stairways and a connecting corridor, almost certainly have much higher costs than benefits. But many other requirements, such as energy, wind, and earthquake requirements, likely have benefits that exceed their costs, in some cases substantially. The data here is pretty thin, however, and it’s hard to draw any strong conclusions on the costs and benefits of code requirements generally.

This would be a good project for someone to undertake using AI models — a provision-by-provision cost-benefit analysis of the entire building code.

1

NAHB activism is why almost every state has struck the provision requiring fire sprinklers in single-family homes from the IRC when adopting it.

title: Premium: Fault Lines
content:
I’ve generally avoided politics here and the few times that I have done so I’ve received a few pissy emails, but Tuesday night was a wonderful, abundant font of hope in what has been an unspeakably grim two years. 

We have felt land-locked in a suffocating era defined by an oafish, half-hearted fascism that lashes out in random directions, where the cruelty is the point, creating a sensation that nothing good can ever happen again — something amplified by the fact that cynical malcontents have turned everything into a casino or strip-mining operation.

And we’ve watched as the political and social infrastructure has caved to their every demand, the media has enabled them, and the existing systems have empowered them. It’s felt for most of my life that we’d never escape the weight of the eras of Reagan, Clinton and Obama, every time people have been sold further entrenchment in systemic thinking.

Nothing will ever be perfect, and I do not think every wish gets fulfilled. Tuesday night proved that things can change, for the better, and that seemingly-impossible movements can be kneecapped and nearly-entirely collapse in the space of months.

And yes, the Blue Wave could very much lead to the bubble bursting, per Bloomberg’s aptly-named “Big Tech Soars on Bet Dems Will Save AI Spenders From Themselves”:

“The market is acting like this represents the end of the AI buildout,” said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Management. “If that means the hyperscalers aren’t spending ridiculous amounts of money to build out compute, that means they could become cash-flow positive again.”

Exit polls showed that voters strongly oppose new data centers in their communities, Keith Parker, UBS’s head of global macro equity strategy and US equity strategy research, wrote in a note to clients on Wednesday. “The blue wave will have implications for equities, with the biggest impact likely coming from an increase in data center regulation at the state level near-term,” he wrote.

A great deal of the “inevitability” of the AI bubble comes from the assumption that the rich and powerful always get what they want, and that anything they say — even the most deranged and unrealistic things in the world — will simply happen. Things like building 190GW of data centers, or, shit, 7.1GW of data centers just for Sam Altman and OpenAI only make sense when you’re under the assumption that everything in the world is at a fixed point derived from the whims and proclivities of untethered capitalism. 

While nothing has truly shifted yet, we are no longer in a political (or social) climate that rewards backing everything that the tech industry does. Texas is now a thoroughly blue state outside of the state senate, where Republicans still hold a thin majority and are already desperately trying to undermine the powers of the lieutenant-governor before Vikki Goodwin takes over in January, which spells ill for the 57.7GW of planned IT capacity in the state, more than half of which is being built by first-time developers per Bloomberg. Thirty-three separate ballot measures to restrict data centers were passed by voters or were leading as of writing this sentence per Stateline, with 21 municipalities in Ohio alone (one of the fastest-growing data center buildout geographies in the world) voting to restrict them. According to Bloomberg, “...[the] gubernatorial races from Georgia to Ohio and Pennsylvania could leave half of proposed AI data center additions across the US vulnerable to stricter local scrutiny and pushback.”

Per The Information:

In 12 states, the winning or leading candidate for governor has called for a pause on data center development, including Alaska, Georgia, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Mexico, New York, Ohio, Oregon, Texas and Wisconsin. And in even more states, winners have also pledged other restrictions on data centers including ratepayer protections, environmental limits and the elimination of tax incentives for building the facilities.

And of the 24 incoming governors who did not call for a pause, 22 back at least one limit on data centers. Ratepayer protections, which would make sure households don’t shoulder the costs of increased power demand or energy infrastructure buildouts, were nearly universal: 34 of 36 winners support them. And 27 back restrictions relating to water usage or the environment. 

It turns out that people hate data centers, are enraged with the tech industry, are tired of Elon Musk, and don’t want to feel like they are under the thumb of billionaires. The AI industry accidentally created the single-easiest bipartisan talking point by force-feeding rural communities giant, expensive monoliths explicitly built to take their jobs, and now face outright opposition in effectively every state other than the Dakotas, with little or no response other than “uhh, having data centers makes America stronger.”

The hubris of the AI bubble is the belief that it could continue to grow unfettered without seeking the consent of those who have to live with its consequences. The AI bubble threatens to take the jobs of working people, to degrade their working conditions, to increase the cost of living, and to force them to live next to noisy, fume-polluting monstrosities — and those most responsible for the existence of that bubble believe that those most keenly affected by the consequences of the technology and the infrastructure must either meekly acquiesce to their will, or will ultimately come to accept the better wisdom of Altman, Musk, Amodei, et al. 

Those responsible for the profligate splurge in AI-related spending didn’t anticipate that people — voters — would and could say no. And they absolutely fucking did, and in doing so, exposed a vulnerability in the AI bubble that I (and many others) have failed to cover with the due attention it deserved.

The AI bubble is only made possible in a climate of unrestrained capitalism. NVIDIA’s growth is entirely dependent on an unimpeded data center buildout, and without it, there’s little reason to keep buying tens of billions of dollars of GPUs every quarter. Without more capacity, Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI labs are unable to sell their stories based on infinite growth. 

And once that narrative sets in, everything begins to implode.

So, as promised, today’s newsletter is about some of the markets, industries and companies most-exposed to the AI data center capex bubble bursting, the data points to watch closely for signs of collapse, and the things that might cause things to finally fall apart.
